part_a.prompt: Define polymers. Give any two methods of classification of polymers.
part_a.scope: Current R25 topic

blocks.text: Polymers are high-molecular-mass substances made up of many repeating units derived from monomers.

blocks.title: Two methods of classification
items: By origin: natural—cellulose; semi-synthetic—cellulose acetate; synthetic—polyethylene.
By monomer composition: homopolymers—polyethylene; copolymers—Buna-S.

part_a.prompt: Choose any one type of Fiber Reinforced Plastic (FRP) and mention one suitable application based on its properties.
part_a.scope: Current R25 topic

blocks.text: Glass-fibre-reinforced plastic (GFRP) consists of glass fibres embedded in a polymer matrix. It is used for boat hulls because it is lightweight, strong and resistant to corrosion.

part_a.prompt: Write about the role of IR spectroscopy in night-vision security systems.
part_a.scope: Current R25 topic

blocks.text: Warm objects emit infrared radiation. Thermal night-vision cameras detect this radiation and convert temperature differences into visible images, helping detect people and intruders in darkness.

part_a.prompt: What is Raman spectroscopy? Mention one medical application of Raman spectroscopy.
part_a.scope: Current R25 topic

blocks.text: Raman spectroscopy measures the change in frequency of light scattered inelastically by molecules, giving their molecular fingerprint.
Medical application: studying biochemical differences between healthy and tumour tissues to assist tumour detection.

part_b.prompt: Describe green hydrogen and explain the generation of hydrogen by Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolysis method.
part_b.scope: Current R25 topic

blocks.text: Green hydrogen is hydrogen produced by electrolysis of water using electricity from renewable sources such as solar and wind energy.
Construction: a proton-exchange membrane separates the anode and cathode. Water is supplied to the anode, and the electrodes are connected to a renewable-powered DC supply.

blocks.title: Working
items: At the positive anode, water splits into oxygen, hydrogen ions and electrons.
Hydrogen ions pass through the membrane to the negative cathode.
The external DC circuit supplies electrons to the cathode, where hydrogen gas is formed.

part_b.prompt: With a neat diagram, explain the construction and working of a Lithium-ion battery.
part_b.scope: Current R25 topic

blocks.text: Construction: graphite negative electrode, lithium cobalt oxide positive electrode, a non-aqueous lithium-salt electrolyte and a porous separator.

blocks.title: Discharging
items: Lithium ions move through the electrolyte from the negative electrode to the positive electrode.
Electrons flow through the external load, producing electrical current.

blocks.text: Charging: an external supply reverses these reactions and returns lithium ions to the graphite electrode.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define conducting polymers. Explain their classification and write at least two important applications.

blocks.text: Conducting polymers conduct electricity through their conjugated backbone or incorporated conducting materials.

blocks.title: Classification
items: Intrinsically conducting polymers: possess conjugated double bonds. Examples: polyacetylene, polyaniline and polypyrrole. Doping increases conductivity.
p-type doping removes electrons; n-type doping adds electrons.
Extrinsically conducting polymers: insulating polymers made conducting by adding carbon, metal particles or conducting polymers.

blocks.text: Applications: antistatic coatings, sensors, battery electrodes, electrochromic displays and flexible electronic devices.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Define Shape Memory Polymers (SMPs). Classify them and explain their applications with suitable examples.

blocks.text: Shape-memory polymers retain a temporary shape and recover their permanent shape when exposed to a suitable stimulus.
Working: heat above the transition temperature, deform and cool under constraint to fix the temporary shape. Reheating restores the permanent shape.

rows: Conducting-filler composites for actuators and robotic grippers
Magnetic-particle composites heated by a magnetic field
A programmed bent rod recovering its permanent shape in water

blocks.text: Suitable biomedical SMPs are used or investigated for catheters, stents and drug-delivery devices.

parts.prompt: Explain the synthesis, properties, and applications of Kevlar polymer.

blocks.text: Kevlar is an aromatic polyamide prepared by condensation of p-phenylenediamine with terephthalic acid in the simplified reaction scheme, with elimination of water.

blocks.title: Properties
items: High tensile strength and stiffness with low weight.
Good heat and flame resistance.
Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

blocks.text: Applications: bullet-resistant jackets, helmets, ropes, tyre reinforcement, protective clothing and aerospace composites.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What are biodegradable polymers? Give their important features and outline the applications of Polylactic Acid (PLA).

blocks.text: Biodegradable polymers break down through biological activity under suitable environmental conditions.

blocks.title: Features
items: Reduce accumulation of persistent polymer waste.
Contain linkages that can undergo degradation.
Suitable grades can form temporary biomedical products.
Degradation depends on moisture, temperature and biological conditions.

blocks.text: Polylactic acid (PLA) is a biodegradable polyester made from lactic acid obtained by fermentation of carbohydrates.
Applications: packaging films, disposable cups, 3D-printing filament, surgical sutures, drug-delivery systems and tissue scaffolds.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What are nanomaterials? Explain the characterization of nanomaterials using Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM).

blocks.text: Nanomaterials have at least one dimension approximately between 1 and 100 nm.
Principle: STM works on quantum tunnelling of electrons between a sharp conducting tip and a conducting sample.

blocks.title: Working
items: Bring the tip very close to the sample and apply a small bias to produce a tunnelling current.
Move the tip across the surface using a piezoelectric scanner.
In constant-current mode, feedback adjusts the tip height to maintain constant current.
Record the height changes to obtain a surface image.

blocks.text: Uses: studying surface atoms, defects and nanostructures. The sample must provide a conducting path.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how UV-Visible spectroscopy is useful in the analysis of dye pollutants in industrial effluents by taking Methylene blue as an example.

blocks.text: Principle: methylene blue absorbs visible light. Within the working range, absorbance follows Beer–Lambert law.

blocks.title: Procedure
items: Prepare methylene-blue standards of known concentrations.
Set the instrument at the absorption maximum, approximately 664 nm in dilute aqueous solution.
Use a solvent blank and measure the absorbance of each standard.
Plot absorbance against concentration to obtain a calibration graph.
Measure the effluent sample under the same conditions.
Read its concentration from the calibration graph and apply any dilution factor.

blocks.text: UV–Visible spectroscopy is therefore useful for measuring dye concentration and treatment efficiency.

part_b.scope: Current R25 topic

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What are self-healing materials? Explain the working principle of self-healing materials with suitable examples.

blocks.text: Self-healing materials possess a built-in ability to repair damage and restore their performance.

blocks.title: Working principle
items: Triggering: damage activates the healing mechanism.
Transportation: healing material moves into the damaged region.
Chemical repair: polymerisation or bond re-formation closes the crack.

blocks.text: In a microcapsule system, a crack breaks embedded capsules. The healing agent flows into the crack and reacts to form a solid repair. In intrinsic systems, reversible bonds reconnect, often with heating.
Examples: protective coatings, polymer composites, concrete and scratch-repair coatings.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the working principle and applications of an amperometric glucose biosensor.

blocks.text: An amperometric glucose biosensor measures the current produced by an enzyme-catalysed reaction.
Construction: glucose oxidase is immobilised near a working electrode. A reference electrode and current-measuring electronics complete the measuring system.
Gluconolactone reacts with water to form gluconic acid.
The measured current is related to glucose concentration by calibration.
Applications: blood-glucose meters, continuous glucose monitoring, and glucose analysis in food and fermentation processes.

part_b.prompt: What is knocking of an IC engine? Mention its ill effects & how can it be prevented?
part_b.scope: Older R22 supplementary topic; not an explicit current R25 syllabus topic

blocks.text: Knocking in a petrol engine is sudden autoignition of unburnt fuel–air mixture ahead of the normal flame, producing pressure waves and a metallic sound.

blocks.title: Ill effects
items: Noise and vibration.
Loss of power and efficiency.
Overheating and damage to pistons and other parts.

blocks.title: Prevention
items: Use fuel of suitable high octane number.
Maintain correct ignition timing and avoid excessive compression ratio.
Provide effective cooling and prevent carbon deposits.

blocks.text: In a diesel engine, knocking results from excessive ignition delay. Suitable cetane quality, correct injection timing and good atomisation help prevent it.

parts.prompt: What is cathodic protection? Explain about impressed current cathodic protection.

blocks.text: Cathodic protection prevents corrosion by making the metal structure the cathode.

blocks.title: Impressed-current method
items: Connect the structure to the negative terminal of a DC supply.
Connect a suitable auxiliary anode to the positive terminal and place both in contact with the electrolyte.

Oxidation occurs at the auxiliary anode. Adjust the protective current to suit the structure.

blocks.text: Applications: long pipelines, storage tanks and marine structures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Passivity of a metal leads to more corrosion resistance. Why?

blocks.text: Passivity is the condition in which a metal shows much greater corrosion resistance than expected from its position in the galvanic series.

blocks.title: Reason
items: A thin, adherent and relatively non-porous oxide film forms on the surface.
The film separates the metal from the corrosive environment.
It restricts transport of reacting species and reduces further dissolution.
In suitable oxidising conditions, the film can re-form after minor damage.

blocks.text: Examples: Al₂O₃ on aluminium and chromium-rich oxide on stainless steel. Chlorides or unsuitable conditions can break down the film and cause local attack.

part_b.prompt: Explain the mechanism involved in the rusting of iron based on wet theory of corrosion.
part_b.scope: Original R22 Unit IV · maps to R25 Unit II (corrosion)

blocks.text: Wet or electrochemical corrosion occurs when a metal contacts moisture or an electrolyte. Anodic and cathodic regions develop on the surface. Metal dissolves at the anode, electrons travel through the metal, and reduction occurs at the cathode.
Hydrogen-evolution mechanism: in an acidic, poorly aerated medium, hydrogen ions accept electrons at the cathode.
Oxygen-absorption mechanism: in aerated neutral or alkaline water, dissolved oxygen accepts electrons at cathodic regions.
Ferric hydroxide undergoes dehydration and ageing to form hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (rust). Rust is porous and non-protective, allowing corrosion to continue.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Discuss the construction and working principle of a typical biosensors?

blocks.text: A biosensor combines a biological recognition element with a transducer to detect an analyte.

blocks.title: Construction
items: Bioreceptor: enzyme, antibody, cell or nucleic acid that recognises the analyte.
Transducer: converts the biological response into a measurable signal.
Signal processor: amplifies and processes the signal.
Display: shows the calibrated result.

blocks.text: Working: the analyte interacts with the bioreceptor, producing a change in current, potential, heat, light or mass. The transducer detects this change; the processed signal gives analyte concentration.
Example: glucose oxidase in a glucose biosensor.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the mechanism involved in equipment, exposed to extreme operational conditions like hypoid gears.

blocks.text: Hypoid gears operate under high load and considerable sliding, producing high local temperatures. They require extreme-pressure lubrication.

blocks.title: Mechanism
items: Severe load and temperature can break the ordinary lubricant film.
Suitable sulphur- or phosphorus-containing additives react with the hot metal surface.
Protective films, such as metal sulphides or phosphates, form at contact points.
These films shear more readily than the metal, preventing welding, scoring and seizure.

blocks.text: Applications: hypoid gears, heavily loaded gear systems and severe metal-forming operations.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Water line corrosion

blocks.text: Differential-aeration corrosion occurs when different regions of a metal receive unequal oxygen. The less-aerated region becomes the anode and corrodes; the more-aerated region becomes the cathode.

blocks.title: Waterline corrosion
items: In a partly filled steel tank, water near the surface contains more dissolved oxygen.
The less-aerated region just below the waterline acts as the anode.
The oxygen-rich region acts as the cathode.
Corrosion is concentrated below the waterline.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: pitting corrosion

blocks.text: Pitting is highly localised corrosion producing small holes or pits.

blocks.title: Mechanism
items: A protective film breaks down at a small region.
The exposed region becomes a small anode; the large surrounding surface acts as the cathode.
High anodic current density causes rapid local penetration.
Restricted oxygen supply and aggressive ions inside the pit help sustain attack.

blocks.text: Pitting is dangerous because deep penetration can occur with little overall metal loss.

part_b.prompt: Explain in detail the following mechanisms of lubrication
part_b.scope: Older R22 supplementary topic; not an explicit current R25 syllabus topic

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Thick film lubrication

blocks.text: Thick-film or hydrodynamic lubrication uses a continuous liquid film to separate the moving surfaces.

blocks.title: Mechanism
items: Lubricant fills surface irregularities and forms a continuous separating film.
Relative motion draws oil into the gap, developing pressure that supports the load.
Direct metal-to-metal contact is prevented.
Friction occurs mainly between layers of lubricant, reducing wear.

blocks.text: Conditions: adequate speed and low-to-moderate load. The oil must have suitable viscosity and a continuous supply.
Example: a shaft running in a well-lubricated bearing; delicate machinery such as watches, clocks and sewing machines.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Boundary lubrication/thin film lubrication

blocks.text: Boundary or thin-film lubrication occurs when a complete thick film cannot be maintained, particularly at low speed, high load, or during starting and stopping.

blocks.title: Mechanism
items: Polar lubricant molecules attach to the metal surface by physical or chemical adsorption.
Their polar ends attach to the metal and hydrocarbon chains extend outward.
These adherent thin layers reduce direct metal contact.
Sliding occurs between the lubricant layers, reducing friction, wear and seizure.

blocks.text: Requirements: high oiliness and strong adhesion. Fatty oils and suitably formulated blended oils provide boundary lubrication.
Examples: heavily loaded, slowly moving bearings and machinery during startup/shutdown.
